questions.module: Valuation and Analysis of Bonds with Embedded Options
questions.los: Valuing a callable bond on a binomial tree
questions.stem: Based on the binomial interest rate tree, the value of Bond A is closest to:

explanations.A: A is correct because we start at the end of the tree and work backwards to determine the value at each node recognizing that if the value is greater than 100, it is optimal to call the bond at par (i.e., it is optimal to call the bond at par if the future 1-year rate is less than the coupon of 5%). Because this is a 2-year bond, the relevant rates to use are the Year 0 (2%) and Year 1 rates (4.08% and 6.09%). We start at the end of the interest rate tree, where the bond makes a payment of 105 (principal plus coupon). Interest rates at Year 1 are 6.09% and 4.08% and Year 1 values are computed as follows: At a rate of 6.09%, the bond value is 105/1.0609 = 98.97. At a rate of 4.08%, the value would be 105/1.0408 = 100.88 and the bond would be called at its par value of 100. Year 1 values are then 98.97 and 100. Working backwards to Year 0, with a rate of 2%, we discount the Year 1 values (plus the $5 coupon) to arrive at two values: (100 + 5)/1.02 = 102.9412; (98.97 + 5)/1.02 = 101.9339. With equal probabilities, the value at Year 0 is then the equally weighted average which is 102.4375 or 102.44.
explanations.B: See correct answer A.
explanations.C: See correct answer A.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: Backward-induct; at each Year-1 node, if the value > 100 the issuer calls, so cap value at 100 (call when rate < 5% coupon)

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: Issuer's call caps the node value at 100 (the opposite of a put); add the $5 coupon at each node before discounting at 2%.

questions.module: Valuation and Analysis of Bonds with Embedded Options
questions.los: Effective convexity of a putable bond cannot be negative
questions.stem: The effective convexity of Bond B:

choices.B: will become negative if the rate in Year 1 is less than the bond's coupon.
choices.C: will become negative if the rate in Year 1 is greater than the bond's coupon.

explanations.A: A is correct because an option-free bond has positive convexity, and the addition of the right to put the bond back to the issuing firm reinforces this. Consequently, the convexity of Bond B which is a putable bond cannot be negative.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because unlike a callable bond, the putable bond B cannot have an effective convexity that is negative. If the Year 1 rate is less than the coupon, the bond would sell at a premium and the put option would not be exercised, effectively making the bond behave like a straight bond (that would have positive convexity).
explanations.C: C is incorrect because unlike a callable bond, the putable bond B cannot have an effective convexity that is negative. If the Year 1 rate is greater than the coupon, the put option would be in the money and simply provides a floor for its price without affecting the upside price appreciation.

questions.module: Valuation and Analysis of Bonds with Embedded Options
questions.los: Effect of higher volatility on a callable bond's OAS
questions.stem: Under Plessinger's scenario, the OAS of the corporate bond will:

explanations.A: A is correct because under her scenario Plessinger assumes an increase in interest rate volatility (from 20% to 25%) which will lead to a decrease in the callable bond's OAS. We can see this by examining the bond's Z-spread. At zero volatility, the OAS is the Z-spread. For a bond with an embedded option, the Z-spread will capture differences in credit risk, liquidity and optionality relative to the benchmark curve. Increasing the interest rate volatility will increase the value of the embedded option and since we keep the bond price fixed (Z-spread is fixed too), the remaining spread (i.e., the OAS) must decline since Z-spread = OAS + option cost. The OAS is the spread remaining adjusted for the cost of the option.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because an increase in the assumed interest rate volatility leads to a decrease in the OAS for the callable bond.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because an increase in the assumed interest rate volatility leads to a decrease in the OAS for the callable bond.

questions.module: Valuation and Analysis of Bonds with Embedded Options
questions.stem: The value of the capped floating rate bond analyzed by Plessinger is:

explanations.A: A is correct because the capped floater will have its rate limited to 5% and there are instances where the rate could be greater than 5%. The case text states the following: The floater's coupon pays the one-year reference rate annually, set in arrears, and is capped at 5.0%. To evaluate the default-free capped floater we must look at the exhibit that shows the evolution of 1-year rates based on a volatility of 20% and the spot rates from the exhibit. There are two instances where the cap would be in force; in Year 1 if rates are 6.09% and in Year 2 if rates are 7.32%. In both of these instances the floating rate bond will have a value less than its par value of 100. Working backwards, we will arrive at a value less than 100. In the absence of the cap, the floating rate bond would sell at par at each annual reset date.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because there are cases where the cap will be in effect and as a result the floating rate bond will sell for less than its par value. While the spot rates in the exhibit are all less than the 5% cap, it is the evolution of 1-year rates in the binomial interest rate tree that is used to evaluate the cap and in this case there are rates which exceed the cap.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because in this case, the capped floating rate bond cannot sell for more than its par value. With the presence of the 5% cap, the capped floater will sell for less than its par value.

questions.los: Choosing FCFF three-stage for changing capital structure
questions.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate approach to use for valuing Firm A?

explanations.A: A is incorrect because earnings growth follows a three-stage model and FCFF is preferred over FCFE when capital structure is expected to change. Three stages: Since Firm A's earnings will go through a period of gradual decline between the high growth phase and stable growth phase, the overall growth regime is best characterized with three stages. FCFF: FCFE is not appropriate when capital structure is expected to change. For Firm A, highly fluctuating amounts of net borrowing is expected due to primarily debt-financed aggressive growth strategy. Therefore, FCFF is more appropriate than FCFE.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because FCFE is not appropriate when capital structure is expected to change. For Firm A, highly fluctuating amounts of net borrowing is expected due to primarily debt-financed aggressive growth strategy. Therefore, FCFF is more appropriate than FCFE.
explanations.C: C is correct because earnings growth follows a three-stage model and FCFF is preferred over FCFE when capital structure is expected to change. Three stages: A common model is a three-stage model with constant growth rates in Stages 1 and 3 and a declining growth rate in Stage 2. Since Firm A's earnings will go through a period of gradual decline between the high growth phase and stable growth phase, the overall growth regime is best characterized with three stages. 1) Stage 1 (high growth stage): Next three years characterized 25%-35% annual growth. 2) Stage 2 (declining growth stage): Period where annual growth rate declines to stable growth level of 2%. 3) Stage 3 (stable growth stage): Time period where annual growth rate is stabilized at the long-term sustainable rate of 2%. In addition, three-stage models are often considered to be good approximations for cash flow streams that, in reality, fluctuate from year to year. Consistently, McCormick's expectations suggest that Firm A's earnings are expected to fluctuate due to the management's aggressive growth strategy. FCFF: Finally, if a company’s capital structure is relatively stable, using FCFE to value equity is more direct and simpler than using FCFF. The FCFF model is often chosen, however, in two other cases: [1] A levered company with negative FCFE and [2] A levered company with a changing capital structure. For Firm A, highly fluctuating amounts of net borrowing is expected due to primarily debt-financed aggressive growth strategy. Therefore, FCFF is more appropriate than FCFE.

questions.stem: Firm B's FCFE (in $ millions) is closest to:

explanations.A: See correct answer C.
explanations.B: See correct answer C.
explanations.C: C is correct because Free cash flow to equity (FCFE) can be calculated starting from cash flow from operations (CFO). FCFE = CFO – FCInv + Net borrowing where, CFO: Cash flow from operations = 535; FCInv: Investment in fixed capital = 110; Net borrowing = 65. FCFE = 535 – 110 + 65 = 490.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: FCFE = CFO – FCInv + Net borrowing

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: Starting from CFO, interest expense is NOT added back (it is not in CFO for equity holders); just subtract FCInv and add net borrowing.

questions.los: Share issuance does not affect FCFE
questions.stem: Given Firm C's announced change, next year's FCFE forecast will most likely:

explanations.A: A is incorrect because next year's FCFE will not be affected by the common stock issuance. This is because transactions between the company and its shareholders (through cash dividends, share repurchases, and share issuances) do not affect free cash flow.
explanations.B: B is correct because transactions between the company and its shareholders (through cash dividends, share repurchases, and share issuances) do not affect free cash flow. Transactions that involve exchanging cash flows between the firm and shareholders represent the use of FCFE whereas FCFE represents cash flows available to stockholders and is irrelevant to how firm uses its FCFE.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because next year's FCFE will not be affected by the common stock issuance. This is because transactions between the company and its shareholders (through cash dividends, share repurchases, and share issuances) do not affect free cash flow.

questions.los: Equity value from FCFF (add non-operating, subtract debt and preferred)
questions.stem: The intrinsic value of Firm D's equity based on FCFF approach is closest to:

explanations.A: See correct answer B.
explanations.B: B is correct because the intrinsic value of Firm D's equity based on the FCFF approach can be calculated as: Intrinsic value of the equity = Value of operating assets + Value of non-operating assets – Market value of debt – Market value of preferred stock where, Value of operating assets = present value of future FCFF = $800 million; Value of non-operating assets = $75 million; Market value of debt = $250 million; Market value of preferred stock = $150 million. Intrinsic value of the equity = 800 + 75 – 250 – 150 = $475 million.
explanations.C: See correct answer B.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: Equity value = PV(FCFF) + non-operating assets – MV(debt) – MV(preferred)

steps.label: 结果
steps.content: = $475 million

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: Add back the $75m excess (non-operating) cash, then subtract BOTH debt and preferred stock from firm value.

questions.los: Sustainable sales growth: organic (volume + price) vs. currency
questions.stem: The market with the highest sustainable sales growth rate is:

explanations.A: A is incorrect because growth in sales from volume was only 5 percent and price was 0 percent. Growth in net sales was strongly contributed by changes in exchange rate (4 percent). Growth in sales that comes from changes in volume or price is arguably more sustainable than growth in sales that comes from changes in exchange rates.
explanations.B: B is correct because the growth in sales for Malaysia came from change in volume and price. At 4 + 5 = 9 percent, the organic sales growth was the greatest compared to Thailand (5 + 0 = 5) or Hong Kong SAR (–4 + 8 = 4). Growth in sales that comes from changes in volume or price is arguably more sustainable than growth in sales that comes from changes in exchange rates.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because overall sustainable sales growth was 4 percent. Growth in price was the highest at 8 percent, while growth in sales from volume was –4 percent. Thus, overall sustainable sales growth was 8 – 4 = 4 percent. This is lower than the 9 percent reported in Malaysia.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: Sustainable (organic) sales growth = volume growth + price growth (exclude currency effect)

steps.label: 代入
steps.content: Thailand: 5 + 0 = 5%; Malaysia: 4 + 5 = 9%; Hong Kong SAR: –4 + 8 = 4%

steps.label: 结果
steps.content: Malaysia has the highest organic growth at 9%

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: Exclude the foreign-currency component; currency-driven growth (e.g., Thailand's 4%) is not sustainable.

questions.los: Temporal method: translation gain/loss with net monetary liability
questions.stem: For the most recent year, as a result of consolidating Creamy's results, Buttery would recognize a:

choices.A: translation loss in the income statement.
choices.B: translation gain in the income statement.
choices.C: negative translation adjustment in the balance sheet.

explanations.A: A is correct because Creamy had a net monetary liability position and the IDR strengthened against the USD. Using the temporal method, a foreign currency translation loss is recognized in the income statement under these conditions.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because Creamy had a net monetary liability position and the IDR strengthened against the USD. Using the temporal method, a foreign currency translation loss, not gain, is recognized in the income statement under these conditions.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because Creamy had a net monetary liability position and the IDR strengthened against the USD. Using the temporal method, a foreign currency translation loss is recognized in the income statement, not a negative translation adjustment in the balance sheet under these conditions.

questions.los: Temporal method: which ratio is unchanged after translation
questions.stem: Which of the following ratios for Creamy most likely remains unchanged after translation for the most recent year?

explanations.A: A is incorrect because current ratio = current assets / current liabilities and the numerator and denominator are translated using different exchange rates. Current assets comprise both monetary assets (cash, receivables) and non-monetary assets (inventory) and current liabilities tend to be monetary in nature. Most liabilities are monetary liabilities. Under the temporal method, monetary assets and liabilities are translated at the year end rate of 14,000. Inventory is a non-monetary asset and it is translated using the weighted average historical exchange rate when purchased or 14,700. This changes the numerator after translation. The denominator which is current liabilities are mostly monetary and translated at the year end rate of 14,000. Accordingly, the current ratio after translation changes. Inventory is translated at the historical exchange rate under the temporal method.
explanations.B: B is correct because both the numerator and denominator are translated at the same rate resulting in the translated ratio being the same as the ratio in local currency. Under the temporal method, sales is translated using the average rate and COGS is translated at the historical exchange rate that inventory was purchased. Both the average rate and the weighted average historical rate when inventory was purchased rate are 14,700. The numerator and denominator are translated at the same rate. Accordingly, the translated ratio is the same as the ratio calculated using the local currency. Cost of goods sold is translated using the exchange rates that existed when the inventory items assumed to have been sold during the year were acquired.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because the numerator and denominator are translated using different exchange rates. Under the temporal method, sales (the numerator) is translated using the average rate of 14,700. Receivables (the denominator) are monetary assets and translated at the year end rate of 14,000. Accordingly, the ratio after translation changes and is different from the ratio calculated using the local currency.

questions.los: IAS 29 restatement of non-monetary items in hyperinflation
questions.stem: If Tay's expectation is correct, when translating Dairy's current year financial statements, Buttery is required to restate Dairy's:

explanations.A: A is correct because non-monetary assets are restated for changes in the general purchasing power of the monetary unit and then the inflation adjusted statements are translated using the current exchange rate. IFRS require the foreign currency financial statements first to be restated for inflation using the procedures of IAS 29. The restated cost is determined by applying to the historical cost the change in the general price index from the date of acquisition to the balance sheet date. Since inventory is carried at historical cost, the restated cost is determined by applying to the historical cost the change in the general price index from the date of acquisition to the balance sheet date before translation.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because under IAS 29, monetary items (such as cash, accounts receivable and accounts payable) are not restated because they are already expressed in terms of the monetary unit current at the balance sheet date.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because under IAS 29, monetary items (such as cash, accounts receivables and accounts payable) are not restated because they are already expressed in terms of the monetary unit current at the balance sheet date.

questions.module: The Term Structure and Interest Rate Dynamics
questions.stem: Li's observations about the shape of the yield curve are most consistent with the:

explanations.A: A is incorrect because Li’s view of the market is not supported by the preferred habitat theory. Under the preferred habitat theory, investors will strongly prefer to transact within a defined maturity range, but if yields are sufficiently attractive outside that range, they will migrate to the alternative maturities.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because Li’s view of the market is not supported by the liquidity preference theory. Under the liquidity preference theory, forward rates are not unbiased estimates of future spot rates, because investors expect to earn a liquidity premium that increases the farther out on the yield curve they go. The liquidity preference theory is inconsistent with borrower and lender preferences influencing the shape of the yield curve.
explanations.C: C is correct because Li’s view of the market is supported by the segmented markets theory. This theory assumes that investors access the bond market only in specific maturity ranges, and will not move outside those ranges even if yields become more attractive in alternative maturities.

questions.module: The Term Structure and Interest Rate Dynamics
questions.los: Forward rate framework: valuation when future spot < forward
questions.stem: Given his forecast, Li should consider a 5-year zero-coupon bond today to be:

explanations.A: A is correct because if Li’s forecast is correct, bond cash flows are currently being discounted at higher rates than the rates that will be used to discount them in the future, so 5-year bonds are currently undervalued. The current bond value is based on the implied forward rate observed for those final two years, and the bond's value will be higher if that two-year rate is lower in the future.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because a bond will be fairly valued today only if future spot rates equal implied forward rates calculated using today's yield curve. In this case, future spot rates are forecasted to be lower than implied forward rates, which means bond cash flows are presently being discounted at too high a rate, producing a price that is low relative to fair value.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because a bond will be overvalued today only if future spot rates exceed implied forward rates calculated using today's yield curve. In this case, future spot rates are forecasted to be lower than implied forward rates, which means bond cash flows are presently being discounted at too high a rate, producing a price that is low relative to fair value.

questions.module: The Term Structure and Interest Rate Dynamics
questions.los: Riding the yield curve: buy maturity longer than horizon
questions.stem: To implement the strategy for Client A, Li should buy a:

explanations.A: A is incorrect because riding the yield curve involves buying securities with maturities that are greater than the investor’s investment horizon. In this case, the investment horizon is two years, so buying a one-year security would not be correct.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because riding the yield curve involves buying securities with maturities that are greater than the investor’s investment horizon. In this case, the investment horizon is two years, so buying a two-year security would not be correct.
explanations.C: C is correct because riding the yield curve involves buying securities with maturities that are greater than the investor’s investment horizon. In this case, the investment horizon is two years, and the correct security to purchase has a three-year maturity. When the yield curve is upward sloping (as in Exhibit 1) and the investor does not expect a change in its level or shape, conditions are favorable for this strategy. The investor buys a security with a longer maturity than the investment horizon, and sells when the investment horizon date is reached. Assuming an upward-sloping yield curve, the passage of time causes the yield on the bond to decrease, which provides extra return to the investor.

questions.module: The Term Structure and Interest Rate Dynamics
questions.los: Annualizing yield volatility; key rate duration vs. volatility term structure
questions.stem: Are Li's calculation and conclusion related to key rate duration and term structure volatility correct?

choices.B: No, only his annualized volatility estimate is correct
choices.C: No, only his conclusion related to key rate duration and term structure volatility is correct

explanations.A: A is incorrect because although the annualized volatility estimate is calculated correctly, the statement about key rate duration and yield curve volatility is incorrect.
explanations.B: B is correct because the monthly standard deviation of yield curve volatility can be annualized by multiplying it by the square root of 12. So, 3.25% ×12^(1/2) ≈11.26%.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because while it is true that longer-term securities have higher key rate durations, the volatility term structure typically shows that short-term rates are more volatile than long-term rates. Key rate duration measures the effect on a bond's price of a change in yield at a particular point on the yield curve. However, key rate duration does not measure the propensity of rates at different maturities to be volatile.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: Annualized yield volatility = monthly standard deviation × √12; key rate duration ≠ measure of rate volatility

steps.label: 结果
steps.content: Volatility estimate is correct, but the KRD conclusion is wrong → answer B

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: Short-term rates are typically MORE volatile than long-term rates; high KRD does not imply high term-structure volatility.

questions.los: SPE consolidation under IFRS (control) and debt-to-assets
questions.stem: Acme's consolidated debt-to-assets ratio would most likely be:

choices.A: lower under Option 1 compared to Option 2.
choices.B: the same under either Option 1 or Option 2.
choices.C: higher under Option 1 compared to Option 2.

explanations.A: A is incorrect because Acme has the ability to influence the financial and operating policy of the SPE and will absorb any losses the SPE may incur, and is thus exposed to variable returns from the SPE. Therefore, the consolidated balance sheet (of Acme) would look exactly the same as if it borrowed directly against the receivables.
explanations.B: B is correct because IFRS require consolidation if the substance of the relationship indicates control by the sponsor. Under IFRS 10, Consolidated Financial Statements and SIC-12, Consolidation-Special Purpose Entities, the definition of control extends to a broad range of activities. The control concept requires judgment and evaluation of relevant factors to determine whether control exists. Control is present when 1) the investor has the ability to exert influence on the financial and operating policy of the entity; and 2) is exposed, or has rights, to variable returns from its involvement with the investee. Acme has the ability to influence the financial and operating policy of the SPE and will absorb any losses the SPE may incur, and is thus exposed to variable returns from the SPE. Therefore, the consolidated balance sheet (of Acme) would look exactly the same as if it borrowed directly against the receivables.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because IFRS require consolidation if the substance of the relationship indicates control by the sponsor. Acme has the ability to influence the financial and operating policy of the SPE and will absorb any losses the SPE may incur, and is thus exposed to variable returns from the SPE. Therefore, the consolidated balance sheet (of Acme) would look exactly the same as if it borrowed directly against the receivables.

questions.los: Accounting warning signs of net income overstatement
questions.stem: Which observation is most likely a potential accounting warning sign related to the overstatement of net income?

explanations.A: A is incorrect because a higher (not lower) growth rate in receivables compared to revenue is a potential accounting warning sign of overstated or accelerated revenue recognition, which would lead to overstatement of net income.
explanations.B: B is correct because management compensation that is largely tied to financial results is a potential accounting warning sign related to overstated net income.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because longer (not shorter) depreciable lives would be a potential accounting warning sign related to overstated net income.

questions.los: Interpreting Beneish M-score and Altman Z-score trends
questions.stem: The trend in Beneish M-scores and Altman Z-scores most likely indicates that:

choices.A: the likelihood of misreporting and the likelihood of bankruptcy have both increased.
choices.B: the likelihood of misreporting has increased, but the likelihood of bankruptcy has decreased.
choices.C: the likelihood of misreporting has decreased, but the likelihood of bankruptcy has increased.

explanations.A: A is incorrect because higher M-scores (i.e., less negative numbers) indicate an increased probability of earnings manipulation and a higher Z-score is better. Acme's M-scores and Z-scores have both declined steadily. A decline in both M-scores and Z-scores would most likely indicate that the likelihood of misreporting (M-score) has decreased, but the likelihood of bankruptcy (Z-score) has increased.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because higher M-scores (i.e., less negative numbers) indicate an increased probability of earnings manipulation and a higher Z-score is better. Acme's M-scores and Z-scores have both declined steadily. A decline in both M-scores and Z-scores would most likely indicate that the likelihood of misreporting (M-score) has decreased, but the likelihood of bankruptcy (Z-score) has increased.
explanations.C: C is correct because higher M-scores (i.e., less negative numbers) indicate an increased probability of earnings manipulation and a higher Z-score is better. A decline in both M-scores and Z-scores would most likely indicate that the likelihood of misreporting (M-score) has decreased, but the likelihood of bankruptcy (Z-score) has increased.

questions.stem: Acme's cash-flow-based accruals ratio for the most recent year is closest to:

explanations.A: A is correct because the cash-flow-based accruals ratio is computed using the following equation: [NI – (CFO + CFI)]/Average NOA where: NI = net income; CFO = operating cash flow; CFI = investing cash flow; NOA = average net operating assets. Acme's cash-flow-based accruals ratio = [7,050 – (9,826 – 8,410)]/45,894 ≈ 0.1228 ≈ 12.3%.
explanations.B: See correct answer A.
explanations.C: See correct answer A.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: Cash-flow-based accruals ratio = [NI – (CFO + CFI)] / average NOA

steps.label: 陷阱

questions.los: Choosing a model when dividends exceed FCFE
questions.stem: Which of the following valuation models is most appropriate for Firm A?

explanations.A: A is correct because Firm A is planning significant expansion, which will result in dividends exceeding free cash flow to equity. Generally, defining returns as free cash flow and using the FCFE (and FCFF) models are most suitable when the company is dividend-paying but dividends significantly exceed or fall short of free cash flow to equity.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because the residual income model relies on the quality of accounting to be good, so that an analyst can appropriately adjust net income and book value. If the quality of accounting disclosure is good, the analyst may be able to calculate residual income by making appropriate adjustments (to reported net income and book value, in particular). In some cases, the degree of distortion and the quality of accounting disclosure can be such that the application of the residual income model is error-prone.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because Firm A is planning to maintain dividend payments at pre-expansion levels, regardless of future profitability. The DDM is most suitable when the board of directors has established a dividend policy that bears an understandable and consistent relationship to the company’s profitability. The fact that the dividend payout ratio has been stable for the last 10 years is not relevant going forward.

questions.los: Multi-year DDM with terminal price; fair-value band
questions.stem: Based on the dividend discount model, Bala should consider Firm B’s common stock to be:

explanations.A: A is incorrect because the current share price of $19.00 is only 1.6% above the fair value of $18.70. Given ValEwe's valuation policy of considering a stock to be fairly valued if its price is within 2% of its estimated fair value, Firm B should be considered fairly valued.
explanations.B: B is correct because the value of Firm B’s stock is the present value of the expected dividends for the next three years plus the present value of the expected price at the end of Year 3. V0 = D1/(1 + r)1 + D2/(1 + r)2 + D3/(1 + r)3 + P3/(1 + r)3 where: D1 = expected dividend received at the end of Year 1; D2 = expected dividend received at the end of Year 2; D3 = expected dividend received at the end of Year 3; P3 = expected price at the end of Year 3 = $21.50; r = required return on equity = 8.0%. Given a dividend payout ratio of 40% (= 1 – retention ratio = 1 – 60%), D1 = EPS1 × dividend payout ratio = $1.27 × 40% = $0.51; D2 = EPS2 × dividend payout ratio = $1.62 × 40% = $0.65; D3 = EPS3 × dividend payout ratio = $1.91 × 40% = $0.76. V0 = $0.51/(1.08)1 + $0.65/(1.08)2 + $0.76/(1.08)3 + $21.50/(1.08)3 = $18.70. The current share price of $19.00 is only 1.6% above this estimate of $18.70. Given ValEwe's valuation policy of considering a stock to be fairly valued if its price is within 2% of its estimated fair value, Firm B should be considered fairly valued.
explanations.C: C is incorrect because the current price of $19.00 is only 1.6% above the fair value of $18.70. Given ValEwe's valuation policy of considering a stock to be fairly valued if its price is within 2% of its estimated fair value, Firm B should be considered fairly valued.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: V0 = Σ Dt/(1+r)^t + P3/(1+r)^3; Dt = EPSt × payout ratio; payout = 1 – retention = 40%

steps.label: 结果
steps.content: V0 = $18.70; price $19.00 is 1.6% above → within 2% band → fairly valued

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: Payout = 1 – retention (40%), not 60%; the $19.00 vs $18.70 gap (1.6%) is inside the 2% fair-value band.

questions.los: Sustainable growth rate via DuPont (g = b × ROE)
questions.stem: Based on the DuPont model, the sustainable growth rate for Firm C is closest to:

explanations.A: See correct answer C.
explanations.B: See correct answer C.
explanations.C: C is correct because the sustainable growth rate is the rate of dividend (and earnings) growth that can be sustained for a given level of return on equity, assuming that the capital structure is constant through time and that additional common stock is not issued. Based on the DuPont model, the sustainable growth rate can be expressed as a function of profit margin, retention rate, asset turnover, and financial leverage: g = (1 – Dividend Payout Ratio) × Net Profit Margin × Total Asset Turnover × (Total Assets/Equity). For Firm C, g = (1 – 45%) × 11.5% × 0.65 × 2.25 = 9.25%

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: g = retention rate × ROE, with ROE via DuPont = net profit margin × asset turnover × (assets/equity)

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: Retention = 1 – payout (0.55); multiply all three DuPont components for ROE before applying retention.

questions.los: Gordon growth sensitivity when r and g rise equally
questions.stem: Under Bala's sensitivity scenario, Firm C's estimated share price is expected to:

explanations.A: A is incorrect because, although the spread between the cost of equity and the earnings growth rate remains constant, next year’s dividend will increase, thereby resulting in a higher estimated stock price.
explanations.B: See correct answer C.
explanations.C: C is correct because the formula for valuing a firm's common stock with the Gordon growth model is V0 = D0 × (1 + g) / (r – g), where D0 = dividend just paid; g = expected constant growth rate in dividends (or earnings); r = cost of equity. So, if the numerator goes up (g increases) while the denominator stays the same (both r and g increase by the same amount), V0 increases.

questions.los: Credit analysis approaches for a granular homogeneous ABS
questions.stem: Based on the characteristics of the receivables backing the ABS, which credit analysis approach is most appropriate?

explanations.A: A is incorrect because a loan-by-loan approach is more appropriate for non-granular, heterogeneous portfolios. The ABS in the fund portfolio is homogeneous and granular because there are many relatively small receivables in the pool. A loan-by-loan approach would be inefficient because of the large number of basically similar loans.
explanations.B: B is incorrect because short-term structured finance vehicles with granular, homogeneous assets tend to be evaluated using a statistics-based approach to the existing book of loans. If the risk horizon were medium-term, a portfolio-based approach would be more appropriate because the portfolio is not static but changes over time.
explanations.C: C is correct because short-term structured finance vehicles with granular, homogeneous assets tend to be evaluated using a statistics-based approach to the existing book of loans. The credit card ABS is granular, with many small loans relative to the size of the total portfolio. The credit card receivables are also homogeneous, and the risk horizon is short-term. Investors in this type of ABS will base their probability of default on the mean default probability, recovery rate, and variance of a portfolio of borrowers reflecting the distribution of FICO scores within the pool rather than conducting an analysis of individual borrowers. These statistics are sufficient to gauge the key credit metrics of the loan pool and therefore point to a statistics-based approach for credit analysis.

questions.los: Expected 1-year total return under a transition matrix
questions.stem: Based on the 1-year corporate transition matrix, the expected 1-year total return on the Valisker bond is closest to:

explanations.A: A is correct because the expected return on the bond over the next year is its YTM minus the expected percentage change in the bond value over the year. First, we must calculate the expected percentage price change for each possible transition as the product of the modified duration and the change in the spread: From AA to AAA: –2.82 × (0.65% – 0.95%) = +0.846%; From AA to A: –2.82 × (1.20% – 0.95%) = –0.705%; From AA to BBB: –2.82 × (1.80% – 0.95%) = –2.397%; From AA to BB: –2.82 × (3.60% – 0.95%) = –7.473%. The probabilities of migration can now be used to calculate the expected percentage change in the bond value over the year. The expected percentage change in bond value for an AA-rated corporate bond is found by multiplying each expected percentage price change by its respective credit transition probability found in the row associated with the AA rating and summing the products: (0.02 × 0.846%) + (0.88 × 0%) + (0.08 × –0.705%) + (0.014 × –2.397%) + (0.006 × –7.473%) = –0.11788%. Therefore, the expected return on the bond over the next year is its YTM minus 0.11788%: 2.60% – 0.11788% = 2.48212% ~ 2.48%.
explanations.B: See correct answer A.
explanations.C: See correct answer A.

steps.label: 公式
steps.content: Expected return = YTM + Σ [ (–ModDur × Δspread) × probability ] using the AA-rating row

steps.label: 陷阱
steps.content: Δspread is measured from the current AA spread (0.95%); staying AA (prob 0.88) has 0% change; add YTM back.

questions.stem: The upfront premium the fund would receive for purchasing the CDS protection on Gonk Industries is closest to:

explanations.A: See correct answer B.
explanations.B: B is correct because an approximation for the upfront premium is (Credit spread – Fixed coupon rate) × Duration of the CDS. To buy 5-year CDS protection, an investor would have to pay a 500 bps coupon plus the present value of the difference between that coupon and the current market spread (400 bps). In this case, the upfront premium is approximately: Upfront premium % ≈ (Credit spread – Fixed coupon) × Duration = (4.0% – 5.0%) × 4.5 = –4.5%. The upfront premium is then converted to a dollar value: Upfront premium % × Notional = –4.5% × $5,000,000 = –$225,000. Because the company’s credit spread is less than the fixed coupon, the protection seller must pay the upfront premium to the protection buyer.
explanations.C: See correct answer B.

steps.content: Upfront premium % ≈ (credit spread – fixed coupon) × CDS duration; then × notional

steps.label: 结果
steps.content: = –$225,000 (negative → protection buyer RECEIVES it because spread < coupon)

questions.stem: The cash settlement amount for the fund from the Gonk Industries CDS is closest to:

explanations.A: See correct answer B.
explanations.B: B is correct because the cheapest-to-deliver, or lowest-priced, instrument is the 7-year senior unsecured bond trading at 30% of par. Although the 3-year bond trades at a lower price, it is subordinated and, therefore, does not qualify for coverage under the CDS. Note that, even though the reference bond for the CDS is the 5-year bond, the fund will receive payment on the CDS based on the cheapest-to-deliver obligation regardless of maturity. Any debt obligation issued by the borrower that is ranked equal to or higher than the reference obligation with respect to the priority of claims is covered. Loss given default (LGD) = 1 – Recovery rate (%) = 1 – 30% = 70%. Payout amount = LGD × Notional = 70% × $5,000,000 = $3,500,000.
explanations.C: See correct answer B.

questions.los: Cointegration: unit-root tests on two series plus Engle-Granger test on regression residuals
questions.stem: The time series ln(PRIVt) and ln(PUBLt) are cointegrated if the tests performed by Silva:

choices.C: fail to reject all three null hypotheses.

explanations.A: Correct. To be cointegrated, two time series must both have a unit root (fail to reject Null Hypotheses 1 and 2 by a Dickey-Fuller test) AND the residuals of the regression between them must not have a unit root (reject Null Hypothesis 3 by an Engle-Granger Dickey-Fuller test). Only this scenario (both series have a unit root and the error term of the regression does not) corresponds to cointegration.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rejecting Null Hypotheses 1 and 2 would mean neither series has a unit root, so they cannot be cointegrated.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Failing to reject Null Hypothesis 3 means the regression error term has a unit root, so the series are not cointegrated (Scenario 5).

explanations.C: Incorrect. 0.387 is the slope coefficient b1, not the mean-reverting level.

steps.label: Formula
steps.content: Mean-reverting level = b0 / (1 - b1)

steps.label: Trap

questions.los: ARCH(1) test: regress squared residuals on one lag of squared residuals
questions.stem: Do the estimates of the residual regression parameters indicate that the AR(1) model on dln(PUBLt) is misspecified?

choices.B: Yes, because there is evidence of significant serial correlation
choices.C: Yes, because there is evidence of autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (ARCH)

explanations.A: Incorrect. Residual Regression 2 indicates the model exhibits ARCH, hence it is not well specified.
explanations.B: Incorrect. There is no evidence of significant serial correlation: the slope of Residual Regression 1 (t = 0.70) is not statistically different from 0, so we cannot reject the null that the residuals are not autocorrelated.
explanations.C: Correct. Engle's test regresses the squared residuals on a constant and one lag of the squared residuals (et^2 = a0 + a1*et-1^2 + ut); if a1 is significant the series is ARCH(1). For Residual Regression 2 the t-statistic on a1 is 2.94 > critical value 1.97, so the model exhibits ARCH and is misspecified.

questions.los: Feature selection for text data: mutual information
questions.stem: To perform feature selection, Silva should select the tokens with the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Tokens with the lowest term frequency are likely noise features, which Silva wants to remove, not select.
explanations.B: Correct. Mutual information measures how much information a token contributes to a class of text. Tokens that occur more often in a particular class have high MI; selecting the highest-MI tokens keeps the informative features and removes noise.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Highest document frequency tends to identify very common tokens that appear across all classes and carry little discriminating information.

questions.los: Algorithm selection: SVM soft margin for non-linear separability without overfitting

explanations.B: Incorrect. An unconstrained CART makes no assumptions about the training data and can perfectly learn (overfit) it; avoiding overfitting requires regularization such as maximum depth or minimum node population.
explanations.C: Correct. SVM with soft margin classification handles non-linear separability by adding a penalty to the objective function for misclassified training observations, optimizing the trade-off between a wider margin and a lower total error penalty, and is less prone to overfitting.

questions.los: Adding a variable: R^2 and adjusted R^2 behavior (t-stat rule of |1.0|)
questions.stem: Compared to Model 2, Model 3 most likely has a:

choices.A: lower R-squared and a higher adjusted R-squared.

explanations.C: Correct. As independent variables are added, R-squared increases or stays the same. Adjusted R-squared rises if the new coefficient's t-statistic exceeds |1.0| and falls if it is below |1.0|. questions.los: Conditional heteroskedasticity from residual plot; effect on F-test reliability
questions.stem: The most appropriate conclusion to draw from the residual plot for Model 4 is that:

choices.A: the model suffers from unconditional heteroskedasticity.
choices.B: there is a non-linear relationship between ROE and SALES.
choices.C: the F-test for the overall regression significance is unreliable.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Unconditional heteroskedasticity occurs when the error variance is NOT correlated with the independent variables and creates no major inference problems. Here the residual variance rises with SALES, so the variance is correlated with the regressor -- this is conditional, not unconditional, heteroskedasticity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A plot of residuals against a feature does not reveal the nature of the target-feature relationship; the pattern here is about error variance, not non-linearity.
explanations.C: Correct. The residual variance increases with SALES, i.e., the error variance is conditional on the regressor -- conditional heteroskedasticity. This makes the MSE a biased estimator of the true population variance, so the F-test for overall regression significance is unreliable, and it tends to find significant relationships where none exist (more Type I errors).

questions.los: Model evaluation: recall minimizes false negatives (Type II errors)
questions.stem: Which machine-learning model should Aoun choose given his concern about false negatives?

explanations.A: Correct. Recall is the ratio of correctly predicted positives to all actual positives and is the metric to maximize when the cost of false negatives (Type II errors) is high. Model X has the highest recall (0.94 vs 0.90 and 0.82).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Accuracy and F1 score (highest for Model Y) weight false positives and negatives equally; they do not directly address the higher cost of false negatives.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Precision (highest for Model Z) addresses the cost of false positives (Type I errors), the opposite of Aoun's concern.

questions.los: ARCH(1): error variance is time-varying but predictable from prior squared error
questions.stem: Based on Aoun's conclusion regarding the time-series model for Bytewave, the variance of the error term is:

explanations.A: Correct. With ARCH(1) errors, the variance of the error in period t+1 can be predicted in period t because it depends on how large the squared error was in the previous period. Thus the error variance is predictable but not constant.
explanations.B: Incorrect. ARCH errors are by definition not constant (the variance changes with the prior squared error).
explanations.C: Incorrect. ARCH(1) errors are predictable: the variance depends linearly on the previous period's squared error.

questions.los: Covariance stationarity: constant mean, constant variance, constant autocovariance
questions.stem: The first-differenced time series for Circuitcraft's growth in quarterly sales:

explanations.A: Incorrect. In a random walk the best forecast of xt is xt-1. Here b2 = -0.5272 with t = -4.3411 (|t| > 2.0), so b2 is significant and its absolute value is less than 1; xt-1 is not the best forecast in every subsequent period, so the series is not a random walk.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Seasonality would show a significant fourth (quarterly) residual autocorrelation. The largest residual autocorrelation t-statistic is 1.8424 (lag 3) < 2.0, so no autocorrelation differs significantly from 0 and there is no seasonality.
explanations.C: Correct. None of the residual autocorrelations differ significantly from 0 (largest |t| = 1.8424 < 2.0), so the autocovariance is constant. Aoun determines the mean and variance are constant over time. All three requirements of a covariance-stationary series (constant mean, constant variance, constant autocovariance) are satisfied.

questions.los: Breusch-Pagan test for conditional heteroskedasticity (one-tail chi-square)
questions.stem: If Cambo assumes a significance level of 5%, based on the result of the BP test he should conclude that the:

choices.A: statistics of the independent variables are unreliable.
choices.B: residuals do not exhibit conditional heteroskedasticity.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Because the null is not rejected, the model does not have conditional heteroskedasticity and there is no basis to call the statistics unreliable.
explanations.B: Correct. The Breusch-Pagan test is a one-tail (right-tail) chi-square test with k = 3 degrees of freedom; at the 5% level the critical value is 7.815. Because the BP statistic 5.8 < 7.815, the null is not rejected: the residuals do not exhibit conditional heteroskedasticity and the standard errors are unbiased.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Underestimated standard errors would arise if conditional heteroskedasticity were present; here it is not detected.

explanations.C: Correct. Because the forward price is below its no-arbitrage value (F0 < FV(S0)), reverse carry arbitrage applies: buy the forward (step 1), sell the underlying short, and lend the short-sale proceeds at the risk-free rate.

questions.los: FRA cash settlement with discounting at settlement-date floating rate

questions.los: One-period binomial hedge ratio for a put = (P+ - P-)/(S+ - S-)
questions.stem: The optimal hedge ratio for the 1-year expiration European-style put on Sunrise is closest to:

questions.los: BSM assumes European exercise; it undervalues American puts with early-exercise value
questions.stem: The BSM model would most likely undervalue:

choices.A: the put option on Sunrise with 1-year expiration.
choices.B: the put option on Sunrise with 2-year expiration.
choices.C: the call option on Sunset with 2-year expiration.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The 1-year Sunrise put is European; BSM prices European options correctly.
explanations.B: Correct. The 2-year Sunrise put is American. BSM assumes European-style exercise (no early exercise). When the stock price is very low and the put is deep in the money, early exercise has value, so BSM most likely undervalues the American put.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The Sunset option is a European call; early-exercise value is generally not an issue and BSM values it appropriately.

questions.los: Delta hedge is most effective when gamma and vega are lowest
questions.stem: A delta hedge would be most effective for:

explanations.C: Incorrect. Option 3 has the highest gamma (0.0098), so its delta shifts sharply as the underlying moves, making the hedge least stable.

questions.los: Backwardation, basis and calendar spread from spot vs futures prices
questions.stem: Based on the current price data of Fund 1's largest exposures, the most appropriate conclusion is that the:

choices.C: gold market calendar spread is positive.

explanations.C: Incorrect. The gold calendar spread = near-term minus farther-term futures = 1,929.3 - 1,935.6 = -6.3, which is negative, not positive.

questions.los: Fund of funds vs multi-strategy fund: leverage, fee layers, reaction time
questions.stem: Compared to Option 2, Option 1 most likely has:

explanations.A: Correct. Multi-strategy funds (Option 2) tend to use significantly more leverage than most funds of funds (Option 1), which gravitate to modest leverage. So the fund of funds most likely has less leverage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A fund of funds typically has a double layer of fees, whereas in a multi-strategy fund fee netting is handled at the strategy level. The fund of funds has more, not fewer, fee layers.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Because a fund of funds executes strategies across different underlying funds, it has a slower (longer) tactical reaction time than a multi-strategy fund.

questions.los: Appraisal-based index: appraisal lag smooths returns (understated volatility)
questions.stem: Friso's choice of real estate index will most likely result in:

choices.C: higher correlation of returns with the rest of the portfolio.

explanations.A: Correct. An appraisal-based index smooths returns and understates volatility because of the appraisal lag (many properties are not appraised every quarter, so index information is out of date), which is especially pronounced during sudden market shifts.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The smoothing lowers volatility and therefore overstates, not underestimates, the Sharpe ratio.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The appraisal lag smooths the index and gives it a lower, not higher, correlation with other asset classes.

questions.los: REIT vs REOC: distribution requirements and dividend payout
questions.stem: Compared to Rainfall Real Estate, Perpetua Properties most likely has:

explanations.A: Incorrect. As a REIT, Perpetua benefits from tax exemptions (it can deduct dividends paid), effectively exempting it from corporate income tax in many countries, so it does not have a higher effective tax rate.
explanations.B: Correct. As a REIT, Perpetua must distribute 90-100% of its taxable income to shareholders, whereas the REOC (Rainfall) can retain earnings. Therefore Perpetua most likely has a higher dividend payout ratio.
explanations.C: Incorrect. REITs must distribute 90-100% of taxable earnings and have little retained earnings for growth. REOCs, with fewer restrictions and no distribution requirement, have greater flexibility to retain earnings.

questions.los: AFFO as the best measure of a REIT's sustainable dividend-paying capacity
questions.stem: Which of the following measures of income would best meet Friso's key objective in her analysis of Perpetua Properties?

explanations.A: Incorrect. FFO is not a cash flow measure; it excludes the investment and spending needed to sustain cash flow growth and cash flow from financing activities.
explanations.B: Correct. AFFO (funds/cash available for distribution) is a more accurate, cash-focused measure of sustainable economic income than FFO or net income; it considers the capital expenditures needed to maintain the property portfolio and is more reflective of a REIT's dividend-paying ability.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Net income includes many non-cash charges and estimates, so it is not a good measure of a REIT's dividend-paying capacity.

questions.los: Liquid alternatives: incentive fees and redemption frequency vs traditional hedge funds
questions.stem: Do liquid alternative investments most likely meet Chang's requirements?

choices.B: No, they fail to meet Requirement 1
choices.C: No, they fail to meet Requirement 2

explanations.A: Correct. Liquid alts most likely meet both requirements. They typically do not charge incentive fees (in most countries liquid alts are prohibited from charging one), meeting Requirement 1, and they offer daily redemption rights, more frequent than traditional hedge funds, meeting Requirement 2.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Liquid alts typically have no incentive fee, so they meet Requirement 1.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Liquid alts offer daily redemptions -- greater liquidity than traditional hedge funds -- so they meet Requirement 2.

questions.los: Multi-strategy fund vs fund of funds: returns, leverage, redemption gates
questions.stem: Compared to Strategy 2, Strategy 1 most likely has:

explanations.A: Correct. Multi-strategy funds (Strategy 1) have generally outperformed funds of funds (Strategy 2), though with more variance and occasional large losses tied to higher leverage; their advantage comes from flexibility and fast tactical asset allocation within a single fund structure.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Multi-strategy funds tend to use significantly more, not less, leverage than funds of funds.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Multi-strategy funds often impose investor- or fund-level gates on maximum quarterly redemptions, so they do not have fewer gates.

questions.los: Long/short equity: stock selection as the primary source of manager skill
questions.stem: Which factor is most likely the primary source of outperformance for the Strategy 3 manager?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Most long/short equity managers time markets poorly (too net long at highs, not net long enough at lows); market timing is secondary at best.
explanations.B: Correct. Stock selection defines manager skill for most long/short equity managers, with market-timing ability an additive but generally secondary consideration.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Leverage can amplify positions (used mostly by quantitative managers), but it is not the primary source of skill; stock selection is.

questions.los: Strategy best suited to limit drawdowns when combined with a traditional portfolio
questions.stem: Which of the following hedge fund strategies is best suited to meet the plan's drawdown objective?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Event-driven/distressed strategies show high maximum drawdowns when combined with a traditional portfolio and provide little risk reduction.
explanations.B: Correct. When combined with a traditional stock and bond portfolio, opportunistic strategies -- specifically global macro and systematic futures (as well as merger arbitrage and equity market-neutral) -- generate the smallest maximum drawdowns and have low serial autocorrelation (good liquidity), providing risk mitigation even during market stress.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Relative value/convertible arbitrage strategies show high maximum drawdowns and relatively high standard deviations when combined with the traditional portfolio, offering little risk-reduction benefit.

questions.los: Theory of storage: futures > spot implies convenience yield < storage cost
questions.stem: Based on the Theory of Storage, the convenience yield for coffee is:

explanations.A: Correct. The Theory of Storage states futures price = spot price + direct storage costs - convenience yield. Here the coffee futures prices are higher than the spot price, so the convenience yield must be less than the storage cost.
explanations.B: Incorrect. If convenience yield equaled storage cost, the futures price would equal the spot price; here futures exceed spot.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A convenience yield higher than storage cost would make futures prices lower than spot (backwardation); here futures are above spot.

questions.los: Neoclassical steady-state growth rate = TFP growth/labor share + labor force growth
questions.stem: Based on the neoclassical model, the steady-state growth rate for Country A is closest to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 3.8% is just the scaled TFP term (2.1%/0.552) without adding labor force growth.
explanations.B: Correct. Under the neoclassical model the steady-state growth rate = TFP growth scaled by the labor share plus labor force growth: 2.1%/0.552 + 0.9% = 3.804% + 0.9% = 4.70%.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 5.6% adds labor productivity growth (3.5%) rather than correctly scaling TFP growth by the labor share.

steps.label: Formula
steps.content: Steady-state growth = theta/(1 - alpha) + n, where 1 - alpha = labor share = 0.552

questions.los: Labor productivity growth accounting: potential GDP growth = labor force growth + labor productivity growth
questions.stem: Based on the labor productivity growth accounting equation, the potential GDP growth rate of Country B is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 2.0% omits part of the sum.
explanations.B: Correct. Growth in potential GDP = growth in the labor force + growth in labor productivity = 0.5% + 2.3% = 2.8%.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 4.3% double counts by adding TFP growth on top of labor productivity growth.

steps.label: Formula
steps.content: Potential GDP growth = labor force growth + labor productivity growth

steps.label: Inputs
steps.content: Labor force growth = 0.5%; labor productivity growth = 2.3%

questions.los: Endogenous growth model: open trade permanently raises the growth rate
questions.stem: Which of the following models would best support Podlasky's conclusion regarding the impact of removing Country A's trade barriers?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The classical model does not predict a permanent increase in per capita growth from open trade.
explanations.B: Incorrect. In the neoclassical model open trade raises the level of output and speeds convergence but does not permanently raise the growth rate.
explanations.C: Correct. Open trade fosters innovation and, through selection, scale, and backwardness effects, endogenous growth models predict that a more open trade policy will permanently raise the rate of economic growth, matching Podlasky's conclusion of a permanent increase in per capita growth.

questions.los: Output gap implications for long-term equity returns and short-term inflation
questions.stem: Podlasky's revisions to the growth forecasts for Country B most likely imply:

choices.A: lower expected long-term equity returns and higher expected short-term inflation.
choices.B: higher expected long-term equity returns and lower expected short-term inflation.
choices.C: higher expected long-term equity returns and higher expected short-term inflation.

explanations.A: Incorrect. A higher growth rate in potential GDP implies higher, not lower, long-term equity returns.
explanations.B: Correct. A higher estimated growth rate in potential GDP implies higher long-term equity returns, and a lower estimate of short-term GDP growth (below potential) puts downward pressure on inflation, implying lower expected short-term inflation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Short-term GDP growth below potential puts downward, not upward, pressure on inflation, so expected short-term inflation is lower.

questions.los: Triangular arbitrage: compare dealer cross rate with interbank implied cross rate
questions.stem: Based on the dealer's JPY/EUR quote, is there an arbitrage opportunity for the hedge fund?

choices.B: Yes, by purchasing EUR in the interbank market and selling EUR to the dealer
choices.C: Yes, by purchasing EUR from the dealer and selling EUR in the interbank market

explanations.A: Incorrect. There is an arbitrage: the dealer's EUR offer is cheaper than the interbank implied bid.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is the opposite of the profitable trade; buying EUR interbank and selling to the dealer would lose money.
explanations.C: Correct. The interbank implied JPY/EUR is 119.4342/119.5550 (USD/EUR times JPY/USD). The dealer quotes 119.38/119.40, so the fund can buy EUR from the dealer at 119.40 and sell EUR in the interbank market at 119.43 for a profit.

questions.los: Covered interest rate parity forward rate
questions.stem: Based on covered interest rate parity, the 6-month forward USD/NZD exchange rate is closest to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 0.6774 has the interest-rate ratio inverted.
explanations.B: Correct. F(USD/NZD) = S0 * (1 + rUS/2)/(1 + rNZD/2) = 0.6808 * (1 + 0.005/2)/(1 + 0.01/2) = 0.6791. Because NZD has the higher interest rate, it trades at a forward discount.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 0.6825 applies the rate differential in the wrong direction, implying a forward premium for the higher-yielding currency.

explanations.C: Incorrect. 8.75% is the Brazil rate minus the US rate without accounting for the currency move.

questions.los: Warning signs of a currency crisis: FX reserves decline relative to FX turnover
questions.stem: Which of the following conditions would most likely be a warning sign of a currency crisis in Country B?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Large inflows of foreign capital typically precede a crisis; Country B shows a slight decline in foreign investment, not an inflow.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Broad money growth and the ratio of M2 to bank reserves tend to rise before a crisis; here these indicators have declined.
explanations.C: Correct. Foreign exchange reserves tend to decline precipitously as a crisis approaches. The sizable decline in the ratio of FX reserves to average daily FX turnover is the warning sign present in Country B.

questions.los: Growth accounting (Cobb-Douglas): output growth = TFP + alpha*capital growth + (1-alpha)*labor growth
questions.stem: Based on the information given to Team Blue, the estimate of the economy's potential growth rate is closest to:

explanations.A: Correct. Growth accounting: output growth = TFP growth + alpha*capital growth + (1 - alpha)*labor growth = 1.0% + 0.30*2.0% + 0.70*0.5% = 1.0% + 0.6% + 0.35% = 1.95%.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 2.55% mis-weights capital and labor (for example, applying full weights).
explanations.C: Incorrect. 3.50% sums the raw factor growth rates without applying the income shares.

steps.label: Formula
steps.content: Output growth = TFP + alpha*(capital growth) + (1 - alpha)*(labor growth), alpha = 0.30

questions.los: Capital deepening, TFP measurement, and investment's link to the existing capital stock
questions.stem: Which of the points raised by Team Green is most likely correct?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The relationship between growth and R&D spending is not clear-cut: technological innovation raises output in the long run but can cause cyclical slowing through creative destruction (the double-edged nature of innovation).
explanations.B: Incorrect. The statement is reversed: labor productivity growth equals the contribution of capital deepening plus TFP; capital deepening is measured as the difference between labor productivity growth and TFP growth.
explanations.C: Correct. Although long-term sustainable growth cannot rely on pure capital deepening, the impact of investment spending on available capital depends on the existing physical capital stock, which explains the strong cross-country correlation between investment spending and economic growth (the effect is especially large in developing countries with low capital per worker).

questions.los: Convergence concepts: human-capital externalities imply non-convergence
questions.stem: Which of the following convergence concepts is most compatible with Team Purple's conclusion?

explanations.A: Correct. Emphasizing the externalities associated with human capital implies a linear (straight-line) production function and is compatible with non-convergence: the endogenous growth model makes no prediction that convergence should occur, allowing high-income countries with more capital to stay ahead through high rates of investment in knowledge and human capital.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Absolute convergence assumes diminishing marginal returns to capital, which is inconsistent with strong human-capital externalities.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Conditional convergence also assumes diminishing marginal returns to capital (conditional on the same saving rate, population growth, and production function), inconsistent with the emphasis on human-capital externalities.

questions.los: Capital flows and convergence: adjustment dynamics under open trade
questions.stem: Which of the following descriptions provided by Team Orange is consistent with Smith's conclusion?

explanations.A: Incorrect. During the transition, growth in the capital-exporting (developed) countries will be below, not above, the steady state.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Because capital flows are matched by offsetting trade flows, developed countries that export capital will tend to run trade surpluses, not deficits.
explanations.C: Correct. Developing countries have less capital per worker and a higher marginal product of capital, so the rate of return on investments is higher in low capital-to-labor countries and lower in countries with high capital-to-labor ratios, consistent with Smith's conclusion.

questions.los: Mark-to-market of a forward via an offsetting forward, discounted to the valuation date

Cash flow at settlement = (1.2465 - 1.245442)*10M = USD 10,580. Discount at the two-month USD Libor: 10,580/(1 + 0.0025*(2/12)) = USD 10,576.
explanations.B: Incorrect. USD 14,964 uses the spot rate (1.25) rather than the offsetting forward rate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. USD 10,557 discounts at the wrong Libor tenor.

questions.los: Uncovered interest rate parity: expected FX change equals the interest rate differential
questions.stem: Based on uncovered interest rate parity, the expected change in the USD/GBP rate in one year is closest to:

explanations.A: Correct. Under uncovered interest rate parity the expected change in USD/GBP equals the interest rate differential (US minus UK) = 0.55% - 1.75% = -1.2%. Because the UK (base currency) has the higher rate, GBP is expected to depreciate 1.2% against the USD.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The direction is wrong: the higher-yield currency (GBP) is expected to depreciate, so USD/GBP falls.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 1.05% uses an incorrect interest rate differential.

steps.label: Formula
steps.content: Expected % change in USD/GBP = i(USD) - i(GBP)

steps.label: Inputs
steps.content: 1-year USD Libor = 0.55%; 1-year GBP Libor = 1.75%

steps.label: Result

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e., this statement is true). In the endogenous growth model the economy does not converge to a steady-state rate of growth.

Max Busse is an analyst in the research department of a large hedge fund. He was recently asked to develop a model to predict the future exchange rate between two currencies. Busse gathers monthly exchange rate data from the most recent 10-year period and runs a regression based on the following AR(1) model specification:
Regression 1: xt = b0 + b1xt-1 + εt, where xt is the exchange rate at time t.

Conclusion 1: The variance of xt increases over time.
Conclusion 2: The mean-reverting level is undefined.

Exhibit 1 shows the regression results.
Busse decides that he will need to test the data for nonstationarity using a Dickey-Fuller test. To do so, he knows he must model a transformed version of Regression 1.

questions.stem: Which of Busse's conclusions regarding the exchange rate time series is consistent with both the properties of a covariance-stationary time series and the properties of a random walk?
questions.explanation:
解析
A random walk can be described by the equation xt = b0 + b1xt-1 + εt, where b0 = 0 and b1 = 1. So b0 = 0 is a characteristic of a random walk time series. A covariance-stationary series must satisfy the following three requirements:
1. The expected value of the time series must be constant and finite in all periods.
2. The variance of the time series must be constant and finite in all periods.
3. The covariance of the time series with itself for a fixed number of periods in the past or future must be constant and finite in all periods.
b0 = 0 does not violate any of these three requirements and is thus consistent with the properties of a covariance-stationary time series.

questions.explanation:

As a result, neither the intercept nor the coefficient on the first lag of the first-differenced exchange rate in Regression 2 differs significantly from zero. Also, the residual autocorrelations do not differ significantly from zero. As a result, Regression 2 can be reduced to yt = εt with a mean-reverting level of b0/(1 - b1) = 0/1 = 0. Therefore, the variance of yt in each period is Var(εt) = σ2. The fact that the residuals are not autocorrelated is consistent with the covariance of the times series, with itself being constant and finite at different lags. Because the variance and the mean of yt are constant and finite in each period, we can also conclude that yt is covariance stationary.

3 Alef Associates manages a long-only fund specializing in global smallcap equities. Since its founding a decade ago, Alef maintains a portfolio of 100 stocks (out of an eligible universe of about 10,000 stocks). Some of these holdings are the result of screening the universe for attractive stocks based on several ratios that use readily available market and accounting data; others are the result of investment ideas generated by Alef’s professional staff of five securities analysts and two portfolio managers.
Although Alef’s investment performance has been good, its Chief Investment Officer, Paul Moresanu, is contemplating a change in the investment process aimed at achieving even better returns. After attending multiple workshops and being approached by data vendors, Moresanu feels that data science should play a role in the way Alef selects its investments. He has also noticed that much of Alef’s past outperformance is due to stocks that became takeover targets. After some research and reflection, Moresanu writes the following email to the Alef’s CEO.
Subject: Investment Process Reorganization
I have been thinking about modernizing the way we select stock investments. Given that our past success has put Alef Associates in an excellent financial position, now seems to be a good time to invest in our future. What I propose is that we continue managing a portfolio of 100 global small-cap stocks but restructure our process to benefit from machine learning (ML). Importantly, the new process will still allow a role for human insight, for example, in providing domain knowledge. In addition, I think we should make a special effort to identify companies that are likely to be acquired. Specifically, I suggest following the four steps which would be repeated every quarter.
Step 1 We apply ML techniques to a model including fundamental and technical variables (features) to predict next quarter’s return for each of the 100 stocks currently in our portfolio. Then, the 20 stocks with the lowest estimated return are identified for replacement.
Step 2 We utilize ML techniques to divide our investable universe of about 10,000 stocks into 20 different groups, based on a wide variety of the most relevant financial and non-financial characteristics. The idea is to prevent unintended portfolio concentration by selecting stocks from each of these distinct groups.
Step 3 For each of the 20 different groups, we use labeled data to train a model that will predict the five stocks (in any given group) that are most likely to become acquisition targets in the next one year.
Step 4 Our five experienced securities analysts are each assigned four of the groups, and then each analyst selects their one best stock pick from each of their assigned groups. These 20 “high-conviction” stocks will be added to our portfolio (in replacement of the 20 relatively underperforming stocks to be sold in Step 1).
A couple of additional comments related to the above:Comment 1 The ML algorithms will require large amounts of data. We would first need to explore using free or inexpensive historical datasets and then evaluate their usefulness for the ML-based stock selection processes before deciding on using data that requires subscription.Comment 2 As time passes, we expect to find additional ways to apply ML techniques to refine Alef’s investment processes.What do you think?
Paul Moresanu

The model currently relies only on structured financial data collected from different sources. Schultz thinks the model’s predictive power may be improved by incorporating sentiment data derived from textual analysis of news articles and Twitter content relating to the subject companies.
Schultz and Steele meet to discuss plans for incorporating the sentiment data into the model. They discuss the differences in the steps between building ML models that use traditional structured data and building ML models that use textual big data. Steele tells Schultz:

Steele expresses concern about using Twitter content in the model, noting that research suggests that as much as 10%–15% of social media content is from fake accounts. Schultz tells Steele that she understands her concern but thinks the potential for model improvement outweighs the concern.
Steele begins building a model that combines the structured financial data and the sentiment data. She starts with cleansing and wrangling the raw structured financial data. Exhibit 1 presents a small sample of the raw dataset before cleansing: Each row represents data for a particular firm.
After cleansing the data, Steele then preprocesses the dataset. She creates two new variables: an “Age” variable based on the firm’s IPO date and an “Interest Coverage Ratio” variable equal to EBIT divided by interest expense. She notes that over the full sample dataset, the “Interest Expense” variable ranges from a minimum of 0.2 and a maximum of 12.2, with a mean of 1.1 and a standard deviation of 0.4.
Steele and Schultz then discuss how to preprocess the raw text data. Steele tells Schultz that the process can be completed in the following three steps:

With respect to Step 1, Steele tells Schultz:
I believe I should remove all html tags, punctuations, numbers, and extra white spaces from the data before normalizing them.”
After properly cleansing the raw text data, Steele completes Steps 2 and 3. She then performs exploratory data analysis. To assist in feature selection, she wants to create a visualization that shows the most informative words in the dataset based on their term frequency (TF) values. After creating and analyzing the visualization, Steele is concerned that some tokens are likely to be noise features for ML model training; therefore, she wants to remove them.
Steele and Schultz discuss the importance of feature selection and feature engineering in ML model training. Steele tells Schultz:
Appropriate feature selection is a key factor in minimizing model overfitting, whereas feature engineering tends to prevent model underfitting.”
Once satisfied with the final set of features, Steele selects and runs a model on the training set that classifies the text as having positive sentiment (Class “1” or negative sentiment (Class “0”). 解析
Frequency measures can be used for vocabulary pruning to remove noise features by filtering the tokens with very high and low TF values across all the texts. Noise features are both the most frequent and most sparse (or rare) tokens in the dataset. On one end, noise features can be stop words that are typically present frequently in all the texts across the dataset. On the other end, noise features can be sparse terms that are present in only a few text files. Text classification involves dividing text documents into assigned classes. The frequent tokens strain the ML model to choose a decision boundary among the texts as the terms are present across all the texts (an example of underfitting). The rare tokens mislead the ML model into classifying texts containing the rare terms into a specific class (an example of overfitting). Thus, identifying and removing noise features are critical steps for text classification applications.

Accuracy and F1 score are overall performance measures that give equal weight to false positives and false negatives. Accuracy is considered an appropriate performance measure for balanced datasets, where the number of “1” and “0” classes are equal. F1 score is considered more appropriate than accuracy when there is unequal class distribution in the dataset and it is necessary to measure the equilibrium of precision and recall. Since Dataset XYZ contains an unequal class distribution between positive and negative sentiment sentences, F1 score is the most appropriate performance measure.
Precision is the ratio of correctly predicted positive classes to all predicted positive classes and is useful in situations where the cost of false positives or Type I errors is high. Recall is the ratio of correctly predicted positive classes to all actual positive classes and is useful in situations where the cost of false negatives or Type II errors is high.
